title: The Binomial Distribution
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 2.10 The Binomial Distribution
intro: After this lesson you can check whether a random variable is binomial, calculate $P(X=k)$, $P(X\le k)$ and $P(X\ge k)$, and find and interpret the mean and standard deviation.

moments.title: What a binomial random variable is
moments.text: A discrete random variable that counts the successes in $n$ repeated independent trials, each with success probability $p$.

moments.title: BITS: four conditions
moments.text: Binary, Independent, fixed number of Trials, same probability of Success. All four must hold.

moments.title: Free throws: binomial
moments.text: Eight shots at 78%. Passes all four conditions.

moments.title: Changing probability: not binomial
moments.text: The make probability rises and falls with results, so I and S fail.

moments.title: Candies without replacement: not binomial
moments.text: Drawing 5 from 20 shifts the probability from 25% to about 21% or 26%.

moments.title: Millions of candies: close enough
moments.text: The probability barely moves, so the 10% condition lets you treat it as binomial.

moments.title: Build the distribution by hand
moments.text: Starts with $P(X=0)=0.22^8$, then counts the orderings for 1, 2, 3 makes.

moments.title: Counting combinations
moments.text: The number of ways to place $x$ successes among $n$ trials is $\binom{n}{x}$.

moments.title: $\text{Mean}=np$ and $\text{SD}=\sqrt{np(1-p)}$
moments.text: These formulas work only for a binomial random variable.

moments.title: Binomial distribution in Desmos
moments.text: Inference, Probability Distribution, Binomial. Each dot is $P(X=k)$.

moments.title: Cumulative probability
moments.text: Use the left or right option in Desmos for "at most" and "at least".

moments.title: Name the event, not just the number
moments.text: Write $P(X\ge3)=0.492$, with the variable in context.

moments.title: Interpret the mean and SD
moments.text: Say what is averaged over repeated groups, and how much the count varies.

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: The video says drawing without replacement "violates independence" but the change is negligible for millions of candies. On the AP exam, state the 10% condition instead: when sampling without replacement, n is less than 10% of the population.

questions.obj: Find the probability of no successes in a binomial setting
questions.q: McKenzie makes 78% of her free throws and shoots 8. Assume the shots are independent. Find the probability that she makes none of them.

steps.t: Check that the setting is binomial and name $n$ and $p$.

work.text: Each shot is a make or a miss, the shots are independent, there is a fixed number of shots, and the probability of a make is the same each time.

steps.t: Find the probability of one specific sequence with the required number of successes.

work.text: Missing all eight shots has no successes, so the success factor is $0.78^0=1$, and each of the eight misses has probability $1-0.78=0.22$.

steps.t: Count the sequences with that many successes.

work.text: There is only one way to miss every shot.

steps.t: Multiply the count by the probability of one sequence.

work.text: The probability is very small, which makes sense for a 78% shooter.

questions.answer: The probability that McKenzie makes none of her 8 free throws is about 0.00000549.

questions.obj: Find the probability of a given number of successes
questions.q: McKenzie makes 78% of her free throws and shoots 8. Find the probability that she makes exactly 3 of them.

steps.t: Check that the setting is binomial and name $n$, $p$, and $x$.

work.text: Make or miss, independent shots, a fixed number of shots, and the same probability each time.

steps.t: Find the probability of one specific sequence with 3 makes and 5 misses.

work.text: Each make contributes a factor of 0.78 and each miss a factor of $1-0.78=0.22$, and $n-x=5$.

steps.t: Count the sequences with that many successes.

work.text: There are 56 ways to place 3 makes among the 8 shots.

steps.t: Multiply the count by the probability of one sequence.

work.text: The 56 sequences are different, but each has the same probability.

questions.answer: The probability that McKenzie makes exactly 3 of her 8 free throws is about 0.0137.

questions.obj: Use the binomial formula in a new setting
questions.q: Worldwide, 13% of people are left-handed. In a random group of 20 people, let $H$ be the number who are left-handed. Find the probability that exactly 6 are left-handed.

steps.t: Check that the setting is binomial and name $n$, $p$, and $x$.

work.text: Left-handed or not, independent people, a fixed group of 20, and the same 13% each time. A random group of 20 is far less than 10% of all people.

steps.t: Find the probability of one specific sequence with 6 successes.

work.text: Six left-handed people each contribute 0.13 and the other 14 people each contribute $1-0.13=0.87$.

steps.t: Count the sequences with that many successes.

work.text: This is the number of ways to choose which 6 of the 20 people are left-handed.

steps.t: Multiply the count by the probability of one sequence.

work.text: Technology can find $\dbinom{20}{6}$ and the powers for you, but you need to know why the formula looks this way.

questions.answer: The probability that exactly 6 of the 20 people are left-handed is about 0.0266.

sections.title: Binomial explorer
sections.intro: Change $n$ and $p$. Choose the event, then read the highlighted probability. This is the same picture Desmos draws in the video at 32:22.

stories.ft: A basketball player makes 78% of her free throws, and each shot is independent. She takes $n=8$ shots. Let $X$ be the number she makes, so $p=0.78$.
stories.lh: About 13% of people are left-handed. Pick $n=20$ people at random and let $X$ be the number who are left-handed, so $p=0.13$.

sections.title: Desmos walkthrough
sections.intro: The calculator starts empty. Work through each task in it yourself, the way you would on the exam, then check what you observe.

steps.title: Read one probability
steps.suppose: we want $P(X=6)$ for a group of 20 people when 13% are left-handed.
steps.observe: Each dot is one value of $X$. Tap the dot at 6 to read its probability. The tallest dots are at 2 and 3, and the right side tails off.
do: Press {plus}, then choose {inference}, then [[Probability Distribution]].
Open the distribution list and choose [[Binomial distribution]].
Enter 20 for trials and 0.13 for success probability, then press [[Create Distribution]].
Tap the dot at 6 on the graph to read its probability.

steps.title: At most
steps.observe: The dots for 0 through 4 are highlighted and their total is shown. Compare it with adding the dots one at a time.
do: On the binomial item open [[Cumulative Probability]].
Under REGION choose [[Left]].
Enter 4 in the box.

steps.title: At least
steps.observe: The dots for 3 through 20 are highlighted. Check that the value equals $1-P(X\le2)$, found with the left option.
do: On the binomial item open [[Cumulative Probability]].
Under REGION choose [[Right]].
Enter 3 in the box.

steps.title: At least one
steps.suppose: we want $P(X\ge1)$ and a faster way than adding 20 dots.
steps.observe: The two values agree. The only outcome left out is zero left-handed people.
do: Tap the dot at 0 to read $P(X=0)$.
On a new row type `1-` followed by that value.
Check it: open [[Cumulative Probability]], choose [[Right]] and enter 1.

steps.title: Between two values
steps.observe: The box reads $P(2\le x\le5)$, so both endpoints are included.
steps.expected: $P(2\le X\le5)\approx 0.7169$ with both endpoints included. If your value differs, check which option you chose.
do: On the binomial item open [[Cumulative Probability]].
Under REGION choose [[Inner]].
Enter 2 as the lower bound and 5 as the upper bound.

steps.title: Mean and standard deviation
steps.suppose: we want the mean and standard deviation of $X$.
steps.observe: The mean is 2.6 and the standard deviation is about 1.504, matching the video. The mean sits near the tallest dots.
do: On a new row type `20*0.13` for the mean.
On a new row type `sqrt(20*0.13*0.87)` for the standard deviation.

steps.title: Report the result
steps.suppose: Desmos gives a number for part of a free-response question.
steps.observe: A bare decimal does not earn full credit. The notation and the sentence are part of the answer.
steps.expected: $P(H\ge3)\approx 0.4920$, written with the event and the context.
do: Write the event in symbols, such as $P(H\ge3)=0.492$.
Add a sentence in context: the probability that at least 3 of 20 people are left-handed.

sections.title: Write it so it earns credit

traps.title: Reporting a bare decimal
traps.better: $P(H=6)=0.0266$. The probability that exactly 6 of 20 people are left-handed is about 0.0266.

traps.title: Using $np$ and $\sqrt{np(1-p)}$ on any random variable
traps.better: First justify BITS. The formulas $np$ and $\sqrt{np(1-p)}$ apply only to a binomial random variable.

traps.title: Interpret the mean in context
traps.better: In many random groups of 20 people, the number of left-handed people averages about 2.6.

traps.title: Interpret the standard deviation
traps.better: The number of left-handed people in a group of 20 typically varies from the mean of 2.6 by about 1.5 people.

The number of heads in 12 flips of a fair coin
The heights of 10 randomly chosen students
The number of hearts when 5 cards are drawn from a 52-card deck without replacement
why: There is no fixed number of trials n.
Binary, independent, 12 trials, and p = 0.5 each flip.
Height is not a count of successes.
Without replacement from a small deck changes the probability of a heart, and 5 is more than 10% of 52.

questions.stem: $X$ is binomial with $n=15$ and $p=0.4$. What are the mean and standard deviation of $X$?
why: The variance is 3.6. The SD is its square root.
That uses $1-p$ for the mean.
That omits $p$ or $1-p$ inside the root.

questions.stem: $X$ is binomial with $n=10$ and $p=0.2$. Which is $P(X\ge1)$?
why: That is $P(X=0)$, the event you do not want.
That is $1-P(X=1)$, which leaves out $X=0$ and misreads the event.
That is $p$ for one trial, not the probability for 10 trials.

questions.stem: McKenzie makes 78% of her free throws and shoots 8. Which expression gives P(she makes exactly 3)?
why: This is one specific sequence. It needs the number of orderings.
The exponents are swapped: 3 successes go with $p$.
Combinations × $p^3$ × $(1-p)^5$.
The failures exponent must be $n-x=5$.

questions.stem: A bag holds 20 candies, 5 of them red. You take 5 candies without replacement and count the red ones. Why is the count not binomial?
opts: Each candy is not red or not red, so it is not binary
The probability of red changes from draw to draw because the sample is a large share of the bag
The number of trials is not fixed
The candies are not chosen at random
why: Red or not red is binary.
After one draw, the chance of red drops to 4/19 or rises to 5/19, and 5 is 25% of 20, well over 10%.
The number of draws is 5.
Random selection is not the issue here.

sections.title: Write a full response
sections.prompt: A basketball player makes 70% of her free throws. Assume each shot is independent. She shoots 12 free throws. Let $X$ be the number she makes.
parts: (a) Justify that $X$ is a binomial random variable.
(b) Find the probability that she makes at least 10 free throws.
(c) Calculate and interpret the mean and standard deviation of $X$.
sample: (a) Each shot is binary (make or miss). Shots are independent. The number of trials is fixed at $n=12$. The probability of a make is $p=0.70$ on every shot.
(b) $P(X\ge10)=P(10)+P(11)+P(12)=0.2528$, using a binomial distribution with $n=12$ and $p=0.7$. The probability she makes at least 10 of 12 shots is about 0.2528.
(c) $\mu=12(0.7)=8.4$ and $\sigma=\sqrt{12(0.7)(0.3)}=1.59$. If she shoots 12 free throws many times, she makes 8.4 on average, and the number made typically varies from that mean by about 1.59.
checklist: (a) Names all four conditions in context: binary, independent, 12 trials, $p=0.70$ each shot
(b) Identifies the event $P(X\ge10)$ with a binomial model, $n=12$, $p=0.7$
(c) Mean 8.4 with an interpretation about repeated sets of 12 shots
(c) SD 1.59 with an interpretation of the typical variation in makes
